newsitem.title: DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC OF CONGO: Opposition militants to defy Kabila politics ban.
newsitem.headline: Opposition militants to defy Kabila politics ban.

text.p: Opposition militants said they would defy self-proclaimed President Laurent Kabila's ban on politics with a march in the capital on Wednesday and would follow this up with sit-ins and stay-home protests next week.
But elsewhere in the city of five million people on Tuesday there was little immediate response to the ban with shops, offices and markets open and traffic circulating normally.

Newspapers reported the ban, announced on state television on Monday, but their main headlines focused on reported contacts between the two political sides or exiled Zaire dictator Mobutu Sese Seko blaming and sacking his medicine men.

"Despite the ban, there will be a democratic march (on Wednesday)," said Jean-Marie Vianney Kabukanye, national secretary of the youth wing of the Union for Democracy and Social Progress of veteran opposition leader Etienne Tshisekedi.

"We have not changed Mobutu to replace him with another Mobutu. The man has changed but not the policies," he told Reuters in the opposition stronghold of Limete. Kabila's forces did not try to prevent him giving an earlier news conference.

The statement announcing the ban on politics and marches in Kinshasa said that anyone infringing it would be considered an "enemy of the liberation of the people". It said that the ban would apply until further notice.

"We haven't banned the parties. They exist but they cannot carry out any activities," information ministry spokesman Leyka Moussa Nyembo told Reuters. "The parties stop being active until we have restored a bit of order," he said.
He said the ban was effectively nationwide as it was already in force elsewhere in Africa's third largest nation, which Kabila has renamed the Democratic Republic of Congo.
Opposition activists marched in Kinshasa on Friday and Saturday. Kabila forces fired in the air and took away some protesters. Government officials said they were later released.
Tshisekedi, citing a 1992 vote in a sovereign national conference in what was then Zaire, has doggedly insisted over the years that constitutionally he is prime minister.
Kabila's ministers accuse Tshisekedi of deluding the people to feed his own ambition.
Tshisekedi aides say Kabila has flooded the capital with troops from Rwanda and other neighbours and accuse him of seeking to return to a one-party state.
"Foreign troops must leave as soon as possible or risk appearing like occupation troops," Vianney said.
Kabila aides say he plans to increase the size of the government from 13 to 20 but that there will be no post of prime minister.
Kabila's Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo marched into Kinshasa on May 17. They took up arms in October after denial of Zairean nationality for ethnic Tutsis.
Kabila has said elections, a key demand of the United Nations and many Western nations, will have to wait for two years.

State television reported on Monday that international flights to the capital would resume on Tuesday with a flight by Belgian carrier Sabena. Sabena staff said that no flight was planned before Friday at the earliest.
The television said the river crossing to neighbouring Congo Brazzaville would stay closed until further notice.
